transcript:
Meeting header:
2026-05-28 15:00 UTC — 45m — POC weekly sync (throughput optimization)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Ethan Rossi (Redwood Support), Carlos Ruiz (Mercury CTO), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Sam Bradford (SRE)

Summary: quick perf review of last week's runs, tuning continuous batching and concurrency targets, discussed queueing/backpressure and next steps for a dedicated pilot sizing.

00:00 Jordan Lee: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do the usual sync — short perf recap then tune plan, hey Carlos hows it going
00:08 Carlos Ruiz: good, yeah busy week but we saw the runs, thanks, appreciate it
00:15 Maya Patel: hi all, just to call out quick — logs show the 2x concurrency run had a pretty high tail latency at 99.9th when batching was disabled, so we enabled continuous batching and saw steady token/s improvements
00:32 Priya Nair: sorry can you spell continuous batching? I think our folks called it continous batchin in the notes, ha
00:40 Maya Patel: yup, continuous batching, so the runtime accumulates in-flight requests up to a small micro-batch within the token latency window instead of waiting for a full batch
00:55 Sam Bradford: right, we've been hitting bursty traffic and single-request latency is critical for product flows; tradeoff is cost obviously when you up concurrency
01:10 Jordan Lee: quick numbers from today: baseline hosted run (single req path) ~ 12 reqs/s at p50 ~ 120ms p95 ~ 430ms p99 ~ 980ms; with 4x concurrency and continuous batching p50 ~ 110ms p95 ~ 290ms p99 ~ 520ms and throughput jumped to ~ 38 reqs/s. these are rough from bench CSV I uploaded to the drive link earlier
01:38 Carlos Ruiz: do we have token/s or tokens per GPU numbers? Our cost model needs tokens per GPU hour to compare to our infra budgets
01:45 Maya Patel: yes token/s roughly: baseline 26k tokens/s across the cluster, with batching + quantization to int4 we saw effective tokens/s jump to ~72k tokens/s per instance type we used (A100p3 equiv). note: our profiler shows KV cache warms reduced decode cost by about 12%
02:10 Priya Nair: small nit: the model we used was the 70b-open variant right? we have a slightly different prompt which tends to expand context, so tokens per request vary
02:22 Maya Patel: correct — the bench used 70B-open, seq len 1024, avg tokens per call ~ 350. if your prod prompt is shorter we'll expect higher reqs/s for same GPU
02:34 Jordan Lee: also wanted to highlight queueing: when concurrency is high we saw the internal request queue grow unexpectedly under spiky arrivals; that's where smart queueing + admission control helps — Redwood can apply a soft queue limit that drops or reroutes to a cheaper model when queue length hits threshold
02:55 Sam Bradford: can you explain drop vs reroute? We can't drop in our critical flows, but reroute to a cached response or smaller model might be okay
03:05 Maya Patel: reroute = policy-based fallback to a cheaper model variant or a cached KV prefix; drop = return 429 to caller so upstream can retry. we usually recommend reroute for user-facing flows where approximate answer is ok, and 429 for internal async jobs
03:24 Carlos Ruiz: and how about backpressure to our ingress? we run a Lambda front-end that expects quick failures or queue signals, we need a signal to throttle at the edge rather than pile up
03:35 Jordan Lee: we can expose a queue_length metric + a websocket signal to the edge that actuates rate limiters; alternatively you can use the per-route burst policy which will return early and let your edge back off
03:50 Priya Nair: question on quantization — we saw a quality delta when we shifted to 4-bit, were the tests with int4 quant and which quant library?
04:00 Maya Patel: tests used static post-training quant (PTQ) with Redwood's int4 pipeline (we used q4_k_mixed in the bench). quality drop was minor overall but your eval set had some regressions in entity resolution; we can try a 3-bit mixed config or selective per-layer FP16 for critical layers to recover quality
04:26 Sam Bradford: curious if continuous batching increases p99 due to waiting for batch fill windows? we saw in other runtimes p99 actually worsens
04:35 Maya Patel: good point — continuous batching aims to keep latency budgets small (we cap batch wait to 8ms), but under extremely low arrival rates it won't help; in our tests p99 improved because the arrival pattern had steady microbursts so batching reduced per-token overhead without adding much wait
04:55 Jordan Lee: recommendation: set concurrency target to 4 for your current traffic shape, enable continuous batching with 8ms batch wait, and set soft queue limit at 100 pending requests per instance with reroute policy to the 13B quantized fallback. that got us the 3x throughput improvement in today's bench
05:20 Carlos Ruiz: sounds reasonable, want to try 4x and 8x and see cost delta. what's the expected cost change if we go dedicated? we need predictability for capacity planning
05:32 Jordan Lee: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, so invoice is predictable. based on current bench we estimate you'd need a pool of 6 instances (A100p3 equiv) to hit your peak with headroom — I'll put numbers in the spreadsheet. monthly reserved vs on-demand delta I'll break out in the pricing doc
05:50 Priya Nair: can we re-run with our exact prompt set? the sample bench differed a bit and that may change concurrency sweet spot
05:58 Jordan Lee: yes please send the prompt set or traffic trace; Priya you signaled earlier you'll provide a 48h trace?
06:04 Priya Nair: yes I'll share anonymized trace by end of week
06:10 Maya Patel: for our next run I'll do: 1) concurrency sweep (1,2,4,8), 2) batching on/off, 3) quant int4 vs mixed bit, 4) queue soft limits at 50/100/200 and reroute policy. I'll capture per-instance tokens/s, p50/p95/p99, GPU util, and queue depth timeseries
06:30 Carlos Ruiz: perfect — also can you add a column for 99.9th at the ingress side? our SRE cares about end-to-end from lambda to response
06:38 Ethan Rossi: will include full traces and logs, note there may be some redactions, but we'll push the benchmark CSV and config now to the shared drive
06:45 Sam Bradford: about security — we still need the SOC2 snapshot and network peering checklist before we can sign off on Dedicated trial
06:52 Jordan Lee: yep I'll attach SOC2 docs and a dedicated-only peering checklist; security will follow up for KMS/HSM questions, but for now peering and audit logs are available in Redwood Private/Dedicated
07:05 Carlos Ruiz: timeline — if tests look good we want to move to a 6-week Dedicated pilot beginning mid-June, otherwise extend POC another 2 weeks
07:12 Jordan Lee: noted, plan for follow-up 2026-06-09 to decide finalize pilot sizing
07:18 Priya Nair: quick nit on filenames in the drive — can you standardize bench CSV names with date + config? makes tracking much easier
07:25 Maya Patel: will do, we'll name them like 2026-05-28_bench_concurrency4_batch_on_int4.csv
07:32 Jordan Lee: any other questions?
07:35 Carlos Ruiz: none from me, thanks
07:37 Sam Bradford: none
07:38 Jordan Lee: ok recap of action items: Jordan send pricing + SOC2 + peering checklist; Maya run sweep and upload logs; Priya send traffic trace; Sam confirm peering ownership; we meet 2026-06-09 15:00 UTC. thanks all
07:55 Meeting ends

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard proper nouns and shorthand. Links referenced: drive/benchmarks/2026-05-28_bench_concurrency4_batch_on_int4.csv, drive/security/SOC2_snapshot.pdf, drive/configs/peering_checklist.md
